analysis.one_liner: Requires Congress to pass a law approving each major federal regulation before it can take effect.
analysis.headline: The House passed it 243-165 on July 28, 2015, with 241 of 245 Republicans in favor and only 2 Democrats; the Senate never voted, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2017.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current law, a federal rule takes effect unless Congress affirmatively votes to block it. This bill would flip that: any 'major' rule — one affecting the economy by $100 million or more, or any rule issued under the Affordable Care Act — would have no force unless both the House and Senate passed, and the president signed, a joint resolution approving it. If Congress did nothing within 70 legislative days, the rule would be deemed rejected and could never take effect. A president could let a rule operate temporarily for 90 days in an emergency, but only once.
analysis.who_benefits: Large regulated industries — manufacturers, energy companies, chemical firms, and financial companies — would gain a standing veto over expensive government rules. Any rule projected to cost $100 million or more a year, or any Affordable Care Act rule, would die by default unless Congress affirmatively approved it, something Congress almost never does. The same industries would also gain from required publication of agencies' full cost-benefit analyses and new court review of the process.

how_it_helps.text: Requires a joint resolution of approval, signed by the president, before any major rule may take effect; if Congress does not act within 70 legislative days, the rule is deemed not approved and never takes effect [S3][S4][S5].

Defines 'major rule' broadly: any rule with an annual economic effect of $100 million or more, a major increase in consumer or business costs, significant effects on competition or employment, or any rule issued under the Affordable Care Act [S4][S5].
Supporters' stated purpose is restoring congressional accountability, arguing that agencies make consequential policy decisions Congress never votes on [S2][S5].

Allows a president to let a major rule take effect temporarily, for one 90-day period, if determined necessary for an imminent health or safety threat, criminal law enforcement, national security, or a trade agreement [S3][S5].

analysis.who_pays: Everyone who relies on federal protections carried by major rules — clean air and water standards, workplace safety, food and drug safety, consumer financial protection, and health coverage rules. With divided or busy chambers, most major rules would fail by default within 70 legislative days, leaving protections unenforced even where the underlying statute commands them.

drawbacks.text: The bill makes congressional inaction fatal: a rule is deemed rejected if Congress does not enact an approval resolution within 70 legislative days, and a failed resolution bars any reconsideration in the same Congress — so most major rules would lapse regardless of their merit, including protections Congress itself ordered agencies to write [S5].
The cost of major regulations falls on consumers and businesses through higher prices and compliance burdens, which supporters cite as the reason for a congressional check [S2][S3].

The emergency escape is narrow: a president can suspend the approval requirement only once, for 90 days, per rule — leaving no path for a genuinely needed long-term rule if one chamber refuses to vote [S5].

During floor debate, opponents sought an instruction to ensure rules protecting Social Security and Medicare — against retirement-age increases or Medicare voucherization — could not be blocked by the bill; the House rejected it 167-241 [S7][S8].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The accountability argument is genuine: agencies do issue rules with enormous effects that Congress never votes on. But the design inverts the default so that inaction kills a rule. Congress rarely passes affirmative legislation of any kind, so the practical effect would be that most major rules — on pollution, workplace safety, drug and food safety, and consumer finance — simply never take effect, even when the statute directing them was passed by Congress itself. The benefit is a check on agency power; the cost is a near-blanket freeze on the protections those agencies administer.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it, but the Senate read it twice and placed it on its calendar without ever scheduling a vote, and it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The House passed the bill 243-165 on July 28, 2015, after adopting a committee amendment and rejecting a Democratic motion to recommit aimed at protecting Social Security and Medicare rules [S7][S8].
The vote was almost entirely along party lines: 241 of 245 Republicans voted yes, while just 2 of 188 Democrats joined them [S8].
The Senate received the bill on July 29, 2015, read it twice in December, and placed it on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders — but no vote was ever scheduled [S7].
The 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017, without the Senate ever voting on the bill [S1][S7].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never became law, federal agencies kept their existing authority to issue major rules that take effect unless Congress affirmatively blocks them. The public kept the protections — environmental, workplace, financial, and health rules — that would have faced a default death sentence, while the industries that sought a congressional veto gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: People relying on federal health and safety rules

sides.party_line_note: On final passage, 241 of 245 Republicans voted yes while only 2 of 188 Democrats did — a near-pure party split, with the Democratic motion to recommit failing 167-241 on the same lines [S8].

industries.industry: Large regulated businesses (manufacturing, energy, chemicals, finance)
industries.note: The bill would make every major rule — and any Affordable Care Act rule — die by default unless Congress affirmatively approved it within 70 legislative days, handing these industries a standing way to stop rules on pollution, workplace safety, and consumer protection without ever having to win a public vote. The industries' gain is the loss of protections ordinary people rely on [S3][S4][S5].
